chunks: And that which was narrated is: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Abd al-Ghaffar al-Jazzi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in ihram who is compelled by necessity to eat a dead animal, and he finds it and also finds game (a living animal), so he said: 'He eats the dead animal and leaves the game.'

So it is possible that the meaning of this report is for the one who cannot afford or is unable to pay the fidya (compensation), for whom it is permissible, in the state described, to eat the dead animal. And it is possible that the meaning is if he finds the game while it is not yet slaughtered, for then he eats the dead animal and frees the game (lets it go).

And we said this because if the person in ihram slaughters the game, its ruling is the ruling of the dead animal. And if that is the case and he finds the dead animal, he should restrict himself to it and not slaughter the living one and leave it.

The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: And whoever wears a garment that is not permissible for him to wear, or eats food that is not permissible for him to eat, if he did so intentionally, then upon him is the dam of a sheep. And if he was forgetful or ignorant, then there is nothing upon him.

key_terms.الْفِدَاء: Compensation or redemption payment for breaking ihram restrictions
key_terms.الْمُحْرِمُ: The person in the state of ihram (pilgrimal consecration)
key_terms.دَمُ شَاة: The blood-offering of a sheep, a specific type of compensation in hajj/fiqh

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a pilgrim in ihram who eats a dead animal out of necessity while live game is available?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi elaborates on the principle of necessity (darura) in Ihram, distinguishing between cases where one lacks the means for fidya (compensation) and those where one must choose between eating a dead animal versus slaughting live game, noting that slaughtering live game renders it equivalent to a dead animal. The text further clarifies the liability of 'dam' (sacrifice) for intentional violations of Ihram restrictions, such as wearing prohibited clothing or eating forbidden food, while exempting those who act out of forgetfulness or ignorance, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on intent (niyyah) in penalizing ritual breaches.
